items.note: Larus glacialis: an old name for a white-winged gull. Probably Glaucous Gull (L. glacialis Benicken is usually treated as a synonym of L. hyperboreus), but it may be Iceland Gull in this author's usage. Check.
Name split off from 'Large and small Gulls'; should probably be merged with the Gulls record
Compared to ducks rather than identified; probably Anatidae
'Large Black Cranes' at Rhuvaal in February. In Scotland and Ireland 'crane' often meant Grey Heron, but 'black' doesn't fit; cormorants are possible. Check.
Blue-backed with a white ring at the front of the neck, too small for a Goshawk: possibly Peregrine Falcon or male Hen Harrier. Unresolved.
Large brown hawk: possibly a buzzard or a female or young harrier
'Large' probably sets these apart from Shag; check

Large grey hawk: possibly Goshawk, male Hen Harrier or Peregrine
'Large Kestrel Hawk' stayed until the end of December. Probably a kestrel (perhaps a female); a larger falcon is possible. Check.
Light-coloured with black wing-tips: probably Herring Gull
These reports gloss 'Mountain Thrush' as Ring Ouzel. 'Large' might instead point to Mistle Thrush or Fieldfare.
'Large Puffins' flying south at 7 p.m.: perhaps shearwaters (genus Puffinus) or a larger auk. Not Atlantic Puffin as written. Check.
'The large Shearwater' probably means the Greater Shearwater of the time; Sooty or Cory's Shearwater are possible
Probably Greater Shearwater; Sooty Shearwater is possible. Twenty in one day is a lot; check.

Garbled ('Large- be crisat Owl'); possibly 'Large-horned' or 'Long-eared'. Check the scan.
'Large-Eared Grebe': Slavonian, Black-necked ('Eared') or Great Crested Grebe

'loots' with the editor's '[loons?]'; could be divers or coots. Check.

notes: 350 names mapped (n 1050–1399). Things to check: (1) Unspecified 'Hawk' names are level 'group' ('hawks (diurnal raptors)'), not a family, because the keepers' 'hawks' include falcons as well as Accipitridae. Change to a family if earlier batches did otherwise. (2) Redpolls: I used separate species (Acanthis flammea, cabaret, hornemanni). Recent IOC versions may lump them as 'Redpoll', so check against the IOC version you're using. Also check the IOC genus for Eurasian Dotterel (Charadrius vs Eudromias) and the English names Common House Martin and Eurasian Whimbrel. (3) Look at the scans for these garbles: 1072 'large grey Gate' (Gulls?), 1095, 1141 'Litmete', 1186 'Macepir' and 1193 'Macprs' (Magpie?), 1345 'OEE Plover'. (4) Bare epithets need the preceding genus checked: 1133 linaria, 1196 major, 1237 Melanocephala, 1177 lugubris. (5) Local names that are uncertain: Mackerel Bird (1187–8), Mackerel Cock (taken as Manx Shearwater), Longshanks (1167), Mussel-crackers (1317), Moss Linnet (1270), Mountain Larks (1297), Large Black Cranes (1065), Lestris affinis (1125), Lar. glacialis (1056). (6) Mosscheepers (1273) are mixed between Meadow and Rock Pipit, so check record by record. Mountain Thrush is taken as Ring Ouzel per the text, but the winter flocks (1303) may be Fieldfares. (7) 'Lark(s)' is taken as Eurasian Skylark and 'Mavis'/'musicus'/'native Thrushes' as Song Thrush. (8) Several example texts don't match their name (e.g. 1253, 1104), which may point to misattributed spans in extraction.
